title: Experiment quality signal design notes (route experiments)
body:
Context
- We are adding route-level A/B/n experiments in the routing layer. Console wants a first-class “Quality” line next to latency/cost/error.
- We already run Redwood eval pipelines (prompt sets + scoring) for model onboarding + regression detection. We need to map those to an experiment-scoped quality signal that is:
  (1) understandable in Console
  (2) stable enough to compare variants
  (3) hard to game
  (4) cheap enough to run continuously during experiments

Non-goals (for GA)
- Not building a full statistical significance engine. Console will show deltas and guardrail thresholds; we will provide confidence hints only if they are low-risk (e.g., “insufficient samples”).
- Not supporting customer-supplied custom metrics ingestion in v1.

Key decision we need
- Define what the “Quality” metric means in Console for experiments, and what eval suites (prompt sets + graders) feed it.


1) Definitions: “Quality” vs “Evals”
Proposed Console model:
- Quality is a single normalized score per {route_id, experiment_id, variant_id} over a time window (default 1h / 24h selectable).
- Quality is computed from an eval stream that is *attributed* to the same {experiment_id, variant_id} dimensions as latency/cost.
- Quality is displayed as:
  - absolute score (0–100)
  - delta vs control (in points)
  - guardrail status (OK / Degraded / Breached) with a reason (e.g., “Answer correctness down 3.2 points”).

Important: “Quality” should not be a proxy for “user satisfaction” universally; it is “eval-based quality score on Redwood-managed prompt sets relevant to this route”. We need copy in Console to avoid over-promising.


2) What eval suites to run (v1)
We need a small, stable set of suites that cover common failure modes across chat/generation routes and can be specialized by route type.

2.1 Route types
We currently can classify route configs into one of:
A) General chat assistant / support agent
B) RAG / grounded answering (citations / refusing when unknown)
C) Summarization
D) Extraction / structured output (JSON)
E) Coding / tool-using assistant (function calls)

If we can’t reliably classify, default to “General chat” suite.

2.2 Suite components (building blocks)
We should compose suites from a small set of graders to reduce complexity:
- LLM-as-judge (pairwise or scalar) with calibration + prompt locking
- Rule-based checks (JSON validity, schema match, regex constraints)
- Embedding-based similarity (only when we have high-quality references)
- Grounding checks (citation presence, quote matching) where applicable
- Safety policy checks (refusal / disallowed content) -> note: safety team owns main policy; we can expose “Safety pass rate” as separate metric, not included in “Quality” initially unless PM insists.

2.3 Recommended v1 suites by route type
(Names are placeholders; align with eval-harness naming conventions.)

A) Suite: assistant-core-v1
- Coverage: helpfulness, instruction following, coherence
- Graders:
  - judge_helpfulness_v1 (LLM judge, scalar 1–5)
  - judge_instruction_following_v1 (LLM judge, scalar 1–5)
  - refusal_correctness_v1 (LLM judge + heuristics; penalize inappropriate refusals)
- Output: weighted average scaled to 0–100

B) Suite: rag-grounded-v1
- Coverage: answer relevance + groundedness
- Graders:
  - judge_answer_relevance_v1 (LLM judge 1–5)
  - judge_groundedness_v1 (LLM judge 1–5; requires retrieved context in eval payload)
  - citation_presence_rule_v1 (% with citations when expected)
- Output: weighted average (groundedness weighted highest)

C) Suite: summarize-quality-v1
- Coverage: faithfulness + coverage
- Graders:
  - judge_faithfulness_v1 (LLM judge 1–5)
  - judge_coverage_v1 (LLM judge 1–5)
  - length_target_rule_v1 (soft penalty outside band)

D) Suite: structured-json-v1
- Coverage: validity + schema match + correctness
- Graders:
  - json_validity_rule_v1 (hard fail)
  - json_schema_match_rule_v1 (hard fail if schema provided)
  - judge_field_correctness_v1 (LLM judge 1–5; only on valid JSON)
- Output: validity gate + scaled correctness score

E) Suite: tool-use-v1
- Coverage: tool selection correctness + arguments
- Graders:
  - tool_call_presence_rule_v1 (if required)
  - tool_args_schema_match_rule_v1
  - judge_tool_choice_v1 (LLM judge 1–5)


3) How prompt sets are selected / created
Principle: prompt sets must be stable, representative, and not trivially optimizable by customers.

3.1 Sources of prompts
- Redwood-curated canonical prompt sets per route type (primary for v1)
- Optionally: customer-provided “private eval set” (future). For v1, do not allow customer-supplied prompts to feed the top-level Quality number shown in Console, because it enables cherry-picking.
- Optionally: “shadow prompts” mined from production traffic (future; high privacy risk + complexity). Not in v1.

3.2 Size targets
- Baseline: 200–500 prompts per suite for stability. We will not run all prompts continuously; we’ll sample.
- For per-hour charts, we need enough eval samples per variant to avoid noise.

3.3 Versioning & change management
- Prompt sets and graders must be versioned. Console should show the suite version (e.g., rag-grounded-v1.2) with a changelog link.
- Any changes during an experiment should be treated like a breaking measurement change.
  - Strong recommendation: pin suite version at experiment start, and only change between experiments.


4) Sampling strategy during an experiment
We need to balance cost and bias.

4.1 What gets evaluated
- Two options:
  Option 1: Evaluate a fixed prompt set offline on a schedule (“benchmark mode”).
  Option 2: Evaluate live traffic samples from the experiment (“in situ mode”).

Recommendation for v1: benchmark mode as the primary Quality metric.
- Rationale: lower privacy exposure; stable measurement; less sensitive to traffic mix changes; harder to game by prompting.
- We can still support an “in situ quality checks” feature later for customers who want it.

4.2 How often to run
- Default cadence: every 30 minutes run N prompts per active experiment, per variant.
- N determined by experiment traffic and cost budget.

Proposed default N per variant per run:
- min 25 prompts, target 50 prompts
- cap total eval cost per experiment per hour (set by PM; proposal: $15/hr equivalent compute) with automatic throttling

4.3 Allocating samples across variants
- Ensure each variant gets equal eval sample count (not proportional to traffic split) so small variants still get signal.
- BUT: if a variant is <5% traffic, we should label “low traffic variant” in Console and possibly require manual opt-in to show Quality deltas to prevent over-interpretation.

4.4 Preventing evaluation bias
- Run evals with the same system prompt and tool configuration as the route variant (important for tool-use routes).
- Pin decoding params (temperature, top_p) for eval runs; otherwise noise dominates.


5) Mapping eval outputs to the single Console “Quality” number
We need a stable normalization scheme.

5.1 Proposed computation
- For a given suite S, we compute component scores ci in [0, 1].
- Weighted average: score_raw = sum_i wi * ci (sum wi = 1).
- Convert to 0–100: quality = round(100 * score_raw, 1).

5.2 Choosing weights
- Weights must be preset per suite, not configurable per experiment (v1), to reduce gaming and complexity.
- Example weights:
  assistant-core-v1:
    - helpfulness 0.45
    - instruction_following 0.45
    - refusal_correctness 0.10
  rag-grounded-v1:
    - groundedness 0.55
    - relevance 0.35
    - citation_presence 0.10

5.3 Missing data handling
- If a hard-gate metric fails (e.g., JSON invalid): quality is penalized strongly.
  - Proposed: if json_validity fails => quality contribution for that sample = 0 for structured-json-v1
- If judge output missing / timeout: mark sample “invalid”, exclude from numerator, and track “eval drop rate” separately. If eval drop rate > 5% -> show warning banner (data quality).

5.4 Display logic in Console
- Show quality score and delta vs control.
- Add tooltip: “Computed from Redwood eval suite <suite_name> (<version>) on a fixed prompt set. Not a universal measure of end-user satisfaction.”


6) Guardrails: quality regression alerts
This is the applied-ML part that interacts with SRE/guardrails.

6.1 What we alert on
- Delta vs control (primary): quality_variant - quality_control
- Absolute floor (secondary): quality_variant < threshold

6.2 Default thresholds (proposal; align with product + SRE)
- Soft-stop / Degraded status:
  - quality delta <= -2.0 points sustained for 2 consecutive windows (30m windows)
- Breach (eligible for optional auto-stop if enabled):
  - quality delta <= -5.0 points sustained for 2 consecutive windows
- For low sample size: do not trigger breach; show “insufficient samples” and keep degraded as advisory.

6.3 Sample size rule of thumb
- Minimum 100 scored samples per variant in the last 24h to label delta as “stable”.
- Minimum 30 samples per variant in the last 2h to show a trend line; else trend line is dotted + warning.

Open: These numbers will vary by suite variance; we should calibrate on historical eval runs.


7) Avoiding overfitting and benchmark gaming
Threat model: Customers (or internal teams) may optimize specifically for the fixed prompt set, leading to better Quality but worse real-world performance.

Mitigations (v1)
- Do not expose the full prompt set content in Console.
  - Console can show high-level categories and a few anonymized examples, but not the full list.
- Maintain a hidden holdout set per suite (e.g., 20% prompts) used only for the Quality score.
  - Engineers can debug with the visible set; Quality is computed on holdout or a mix with majority weight on holdout.
  - Important: keep holdout stable for months; rotate slowly and announce changes.
- Rate-limit repeated eval runs for the same experiment if we detect “rapid iteration” behavior:
  - e.g., more than X experiment config changes per hour + repeated evaluation requests.
  - This is more of a product/policy feature; noting it here.
- Use multiple graders with different prompts / judge models to reduce single-point exploitation.
- Pin judge prompts and versions; track judge drift.

Mitigations (post-v1)
- Add “in situ” live-traffic eval sampling using privacy-preserving logging (requires strong approvals).
- Add outcome-based metrics (task success) where tool calls have deterministic success checks.


8) Operational details / integration notes
8.1 Attribution
- Evals output must include {experiment_id, variant_id, route_id, model_id}.
- For benchmark-mode evals, we explicitly set experiment_id/variant_id in the eval run metadata (not derived from router).
- For in situ mode later, attribution comes from request context (same as latency/cost).

8.2 Data model expectations (for Logan/Mei)
- We will publish a compact stream:
  - event_time
  - experiment_id
  - variant_id
  - route_id
  - suite_name
  - suite_version
  - score (0–100)
  - component_scores (optional; v1 can be flattened into separate metric names)
  - eval_status (ok/timeout/invalid)

Note: component_scores as a nested object is convenient but may be a pain for metrics pipelines; fine to emit as multiple rows or columns in analytics tables.

8.3 Cost controls
- Evals must have a budget guard:
  - max tokens per run
  - max concurrent eval jobs per org
  - max hourly spend per active experiment
- Console should show “Quality coverage” and “Eval compute usage” in an advanced section (optional).

8.4 Failure modes
- Judge model outage -> quality freezes and shows “stale” badge.
- Suite version mismatch -> quality should not compare across versions (or must annotate). Ideally pin per experiment.


9) Open questions / TODOs
- [Marissa] Do we want Quality as a single number, or do we show “Quality (overall)” + “Schema validity” separately for structured output routes?
- [Selene] How do we represent “quality regression” vs “expected tradeoff” when customers accept a small quality drop for cost wins? (Maybe allow per-experiment custom guardrail thresholds.)
- [Logan] Telemetry cardinality: suite_name/suite_version tags could explode if not constrained. Propose limited set of suites in v1 and enforce allowlist.
- [Olivia] Where does eval suite selection live? In experiment config? In route config? In Console UI as an optional “attach eval suite” step?
- [Jonas] Calibration: we need baseline distributions per suite across common models to ensure 0–100 feels meaningful.


10) Proposed next steps
- Finalize v1 suite list + weights with PM (Marissa) and Applied ML sponsor (Maya) by end of week.
- Implement holdout prompt set mechanism in eval-harness (if not already supported) and confirm we can keep it non-customer-visible.
- Align on the Console tooltip/copy to avoid over-claiming.
- Provide SRE/guardrails recommended default thresholds + sample size guidance.

Appendix A: Example Console copy (draft)
- “Quality is computed from Redwood-managed evaluation suites run on a fixed prompt set. It is a directional signal for comparing variants and may not fully reflect end-user satisfaction.”

Appendix B: Quick weight table (draft)
assistant-core-v1
- helpfulness: 0.45
- instruction following: 0.45
- refusal correctness: 0.10

rag-grounded-v1
- groundedness: 0.55
- relevance: 0.35
- citation presence: 0.10

structured-json-v1
- json validity gate: hard
- field correctness: 1.00 (only on valid samples)
